The egg dimensions of the Chestnut-winged cuckoo provide a basis for estimating initial offspring mass. Measurements of the calcareous egg indicate a typical length ranging from 25.4 to 29.9 millimeters and a width from 20.3 to 24.4 millimeters, from which the initial wet weight of the newly laid egg is calculated to be approximately 6.84 grams [Ww0 = approximately 6.84 grams]. The nestling period, spent within the nest of a foster parent such as the frequent host Garrulax monileger, is relatively brief. Under the incubation and brooding conditions typical of the breeding season, at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], the young cuckoo achieves its first flight and departs the nest at 18 days after hatching [tx = 18 days after hatching]. This rapid development is characteristic of many brood-parasitic species, which often trade a lengthy dependency for a faster growth trajectory. This pattern of accelerated fledging is especially pronounced in cuckoos, where the parasitic nestling often outcompetes host young for food, allowing a swift transition to independence.

Sexual maturation in Clamator coromandus occurs within a relatively compressed timeframe for a cuckoo of this size. In the same thermal environment of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C] that characterizes the active season, the onset of puberty is documented at 54 days after hatching [tp = 54 days after hatching]. This is followed shortly thereafter by the first successful reproductive event, with the time since birth at first brood recorded at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This pattern suggests that while individuals can attain reproductive condition early, a full annual cycle is required before they engage in their own breeding activities, a timing likely aligned with the seasonal availability of suitable host nests. The species demonstrates a relatively slow pace of life in this regard, with the interval between attainment of sexual maturity and first reproduction spanning nearly a full year.

Female Chestnut-winged cuckoos attain a maximum adult body mass that is markedly greater than their hatching weight. The ultimate wet weight for sexually mature females reaches approximately 75.1 grams [Wwi = approximately 75.1 grams], a figure consistent with the reported range of 66.4 to 86 grams from field measurements. This adult mass contrasts sharply with the initial investment in the egg. The species lays between 3 and 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 3 and 4 eggs per clutch] and typically produces only a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], resulting in a modest annual reproductive output. This low fecundity is a common life-history strategy among obligate brood parasites, where each nesting attempt depends critically on the availability and acceptance by a suitable foster parent.

Basal metabolic rate provides insight into the energetic demands underpinning this species' life cycle. Respirometry trials conducted during the active season at a controlled ambient temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C] yielded a maximum resting metabolic rate of 57.41 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 57.41 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This relatively modest metabolic expenditure for a bird of 75 grams aligns with the energy-conserving lifestyle of a brood parasite, which avoids the considerable costs of nest building, incubation, and extended parental care. The incubation period of the parasitic egg within the host's nest is another critical energetic bottleneck. Based on observations of their frequent host, Garrulax monileger, the age at birth, defined as the hatching event, occurs after 13 days [ab = 13 days] of incubation at approximately 39 °C [T = approximately 39 °C].

The maximum lifespan of the Chestnut-winged cuckoo suggests a life-history strategy favoring adult survival over high annual fecundity. Under typical field conditions, the oldest documented individuals reach approximately 10.6 years [am = approximately 10.6 years] at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This longevity, achieved within the same thermal regime of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C] that governs its active metabolism and reproduction, allows the species ample opportunity for repeated breeding attempts across several seasons, which partly compensates for its single-clutch annual output. The combination of a moderate adult body mass, a reduced metabolic rate, and an extended lifespan positions Clamator coromandus as a relatively slow-living species within the Cuculidae family, where life-history strategies range widely from the short-lived, highly fecund to the more long-lived and iteroparous.
